Childhood non-Hodgkin lymphoma is a disease in which malignant (cancer) cells form in the lymph system.
The lymph system is part of the immune system. It is made up of organs and tissues that make and store cells that fight infection and disease. The organs of the lymph system include the spleen, thymus, tonsils, adenoids, and lymph nodes. The lymph system also includes vessels that carry lymph fluid. Lymph fluid is a clear, watery fluid that contains white blood cells called lymphocytes. Lymphocytes are made in the bone marrow and live in the lymph nodes. They help the body fight infection and disease. The lymph system helps protect the body from germs and other harmful substances. Cancer can start in the lymph system and spread to other parts of the body. There are two main types of childhood non-Hodgkin lymphoma: Burkitt lymphoma and non-Burkitt lymphoma.
Burkitt lymphoma is a fast-growing cancer of the lymph system. It usually starts in the stomach or the back of the mouth. Non-Burkitt lymphoma is a slow-growing cancer of the lymph system. It may start in any part of the body. The most common type of non-Burkitt lymphoma is diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Other types of non-Burkitt lymphoma include follicular lymphoma, lymphoblastic lymphoma, and lymphoma that forms in the brain.
